en.title: Completed and ongoing action: aspect
en.summary: Aspect shows whether an action is seen as finished, in progress or as a result.

paragraphs: Tense places an action in time (past, present or future). Aspect shows how the speaker sees the action: as a simple fact, as something in progress, or as something completed with a result. English has three aspects: simple, continuous and perfect.

items: She **has worked** here for years. (perfect: a result up to now)

blocks.html:
AspectFormMeaningExample
simplebase form or pasta fact, a habit or a complete eventI wrote a letter.
continuousbe + -ingin progress, temporaryI was writing a letter.
perfecthave + participlecompleted, with a link to a later timeI had written a letter.
perfect continuoushave been + -ingin progress up to a timeI have been writing all day.

paragraphs: Compare these two past sentences. The first presents the action as a complete event; the second presents it as an activity in progress, which may not have finished.

blocks.html:
Simple pastPast continuous
I read the book. (all of it)I was reading the book. (I may not have finished)
She painted the room. (the room is painted)She was painting the room. (the work was going on)

paragraphs: Verbs of state, such as know, believe, like and belong, normally take the simple aspect, because they do not describe a process. Compare I know him with I am knowing him (not possible). Some verbs change meaning: I think he is right (opinion); I am thinking about it (process).

items: Wrong: **I am knowing the answer.** Right: **I know the answer.**
Wrong: **I live here since 2020.** Right: **I have lived here since 2020.**
Wrong: **She is having a car.** Right: **She has a car.** (have as possession is a state)
